contentHtml:
Dr Upasana Arora, Managing Director, Yashoda Group of Hospitals, discusses what is driving international patients to India, how hospitals are building a seamless experience for them and what will be required to sustain India’s ambitions as a global healthcare destination

India’s healthcare success story is no longer limited to its people and borders. The country has built one of the most compelling medical value travel (MVT) infrastructures with advanced medical facilities, highly skilled healthcare professionals, and cost-effective treatments.

India today offers an integrated healthcare ecosystem that is attracting international patients who are seeking quality, affordability, and trust. Cost-effective treatments are delivered at globally benchmarked hospitals by renowned specialists, while traditional AYUSH systems add a distinctive preventive and wellness dimension to the country’s medical tourism appeal.

India’s medical tourism industry is expected to reach a value of USD 16.2 billion by 2030, and in 2025 alone, 507,244 foreign nationals arrived in the country specifically for medical treatment. With this trajectory, India is on track to become a global healthcare leader by 2047.

Why patients are opting for India

The attraction for India as an MVT destination goes beyond the aspect of affordability. High-end treatments like cardiac surgery, orthopaedic implants, oncology treatments, and even organ transplants can be offered in India at a mere fraction of what the patient would pay in the USA, the UK, and some regions of the Middle East. Moreover, the quality of treatment in India is similar to international standards. This is enabled by advanced medical technology and skilled specialists, many trained or accredited internationally. Crucially, it also means patients can access specialised treatment without the long waiting periods that have become common in several developed healthcare systems.

What comprehensive international patient care looks like in practice Attracting international patients is only half the equation; the real differentiator is what happens once they arrive or before they even board a flight. Leading Indian hospital networks have recognised that medical value travel succeeds only when clinical excellence is matched by end-to-end patient support.

This has translated into a dedicated international patient services framework built around removing every point of friction from the patient’s journey. It begins well before arrival, with a free phone consultation to match the patient with the right specialist, followed by a detailed treatment cost estimate so families can plan their medical journey with financial clarity. Visa letters, visa extensions, and complimentary airport and hotel pickup and drop-off are arranged so that transportation never becomes a barrier to care. Once in India, professional interpreters well versed in medical jargon ensure that language is not a barrier of communication between patient and doctor, while collaborations with some of the best international insurance companies make it possible for the patients to undergo cashless treatments. The availability of a help desk and an FAQ feature allows the patient to get expert opinions before opting for any treatment plan.

This model combines state-of-the-art infrastructure and internationally trained specialists with structured, human support at every step. This is quietly becoming the norm among India’s leading hospitals, as the country establishes itself as a global healthcare destination that international patients trust over options closer to home. It signals to an anxious patient arriving from another country that they are not just booking a procedure, but entering a system built to help them throughout the journey.

The road ahead

For India to convert its current momentum into lasting global leadership in MVT, the next phase must go beyond individual hospitals doing this well. The government has already taken some steps with “Heal in India” to assist international patients and continue to simplify visa and travel processes. The coordination between government vision and private players will position India not just as a destination patients choose for cost; it will be one they choose for trust.
